facts.text: In November 1935 a fire at a house on Wimpole Street in London killed five women; telephone operators then had difficulty picking out emergency calls from ordinary ones.
A committee that reviewed the problem recommended one emergency number that was easy to remember and could be dialed from a public telephone box without paying.
The first 999 call was made in London on 30 June 1937; at first the service covered only a 12-mile radius around Oxford Circus.
In its first week the 999 service received 1,336 calls.
999 spread to other big British cities after the Second World War and covered the whole UK by 1976.
Today 999 in the UK connects callers to the police, the ambulance service, the fire service and the coastguard.
Before 911, Americans in an emergency usually dialed 0 for an operator or called a local seven-digit number.
A presidential commission recommended a single emergency number in 1967.
On 12 January 1968 the telephone company AT&T announced 911 as a universal emergency number; it used three digits rather than seven so that the number would be easier to remember.
The first 911 call was made on 16 February 1968 in Haleyville, Alabama.
911 service covered 17 percent of the U.S. population in 1976 and 50 percent in 1987.
A 911 call goes to a 24-hour answering center that handles emergency calls for police, fire and ambulance services.
On 29 July 1991 the Council of the European Communities decided to introduce 112 as the single European emergency number, to be in place by 31 December 1992 at the latest.
According to the European Commission, a single number became important as more and more people traveled across borders in Europe.
112 can be called free of charge from fixed and mobile phones anywhere in the EU, reaching police, ambulance or fire services, and it works alongside existing national emergency numbers.
Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Malta, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania and Sweden use 112 as their only national emergency number.
In Japan, 119 has been in use since 1 October 1927 and is used to report fires and call ambulances; the police number 110 has been in use since 1 October 1948.
In Taiwan, 119 is the number for fire and rescue services and 110 is the police number.

In Taiwan, 112 can be dialed from a mobile phone even without a SIM card, as long as the phone has power and a signal; callers press 0 to be connected to the police (110) or 9 to be connected to fire and ambulance services (119).
Taiwan's fire services advise calling 110 or 119 directly when the signal is good, because 112 first plays a recorded menu, which takes extra time.

Derived from the dates above: 911 came into use 31 years after 999 (1968 minus 1937); Japan's 119 began 21 years before its 110 (1948 minus 1927) and 10 years before 999; the EU chose 112 64 years after Japan began using 119 and 54 years after 999.
